questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I wanted to take courses that were of personal interest to me, and were not offered at KU. 
Also, most of my family lives in Canada, and I have gone there a lot, but have never experienced living there before now!

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Of course there were ups and downs, but overall, it was a fantastic time.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: We had an orientation event on the second day of term, which had a lot of helpful information regarding health facilities, clubs, stuff like that.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I got an information packet when I arrived at my residence on campus with a map of campus, emergency numbers etc.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I would have wished for more events for exchange students - we only had one orientation event which all exchange students took part in, but from that moment on, there were no more events organised by Go Global. So you kind of had to find your people yourself!

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: There are many different residences, I was in Walter Gage Apartments, which is a studio, so I lived by myself. Normally, Walter Gage is dorms of six people. I also know of Fairview, which is about ten minutes away from campus on foot, and is more like a house with four people per house.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: I had a little kitchen with a stove, oven, and microwave. There is also a little grocery store on campus (though it's pretty expensive), and the closest supermarket is five minutes away by bus (Save on Foods).

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
I do wish that housing would have supplied bedding and kitchenware, as arriving and not having anything in the apartment was a bit stressful (I should add though that due to a delayed flight I landed quite late, but still would have been nice to have even if I had arrived on time!). You can buy stuff at the Bookstore on campus, but it will be a bit pricey!
Further, make sure to apply asap, and don't wait until right before the deadline to submit your housing application like I did. The earlier you submit your application, the higher on the waiting list you will be in case you are not allocated a spot through the housing lottery!

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The studio I was in was really nice and had everything I needed once I bought the bedding and kitchen stuff. There was no common room for Gage Apartments, so I just usually hung out in the main building of the Walter Gage residence to hang out with people.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was supposed to go on exchange in September 2024, but deferred to January 2025 due to housing issues.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
I was to fill in a preliminary course list as part of my application to UBC. When it was time to actually register classes, a lot of the courses I had wanted to take were either not available, or were simply not taking place. I don't think I knew which courses I was registered for until sometime in July. Whether that was because UBC had switched to a new database (Workday) and things were chaotic because of that, I don't know, but it was quite frustrating. 
When I decided to defer, the course registration was really easy, I just emailed Go Global the new courses I would like to take and they registered them for me right away.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Go Global responded very kindly, and quite quickly, though admittedly during the first registration round for September it took a while to get an answer (I gather because everyone is registering and they get a lot of emails)

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: For September, I got two out of four classes I had wanted, but for January, I actually got all the classes I wanted!

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Have some backup options in mind in case the course you wanted is full/not taking place after all. Don't hesitate to email profs to see if there is any space left in their class - and remember there is a drop and switch survey a few weeks after term starts, so you are not stuck in the classes you chose in case you change your mind!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: All but one class were organised and executed really well (my Japanese prof was incredibly nice and fun, but lacked organization at times)

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
I took two 400 level classes, as they are counted as graduate level at KU. UBC's grad level classes are 500, and those are a bit more complicated to get into, so I just went with the 400s instead. 
Otherwise I took two intro classes!

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was quite similar, but I think mostly because three out of four classes I took were quite small in size, and therefore largely practical and based on discussions. There was definitely a lot less group work. One of my classes was a lecture, so you don't really interact with the teacher at all besides listening which was new!

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Audio Storytelling (400 level) - a mix of science communication and podcasting, so you learn also how to edit audio.
Sociology of the Environment (400 level) - different sociological perspectives on how environmental change affects different people
Intro to Creative Writing (200 level) - intro to different genres, such as fiction, poetry, memoir etc.
Intro to Japanese (100 level) - intro to the hiragana, katakana and some kanji, and basic grammar points

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I really loved Audio Storytelling! I have never taken a class like it before, and really enjoyed being able to present scientific topics not as an academic essay, but in a podcast form. The teachers were incredibly kind, overall an awesome class. 
Also the teacher for the Sociology of the Environment class was incredibly nice and explained things really well, so even for me who had not really had much background in Sociology it was interesting and easy to follow along!

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: If you register for clubs, there is a small fee (5-20 CAD).

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Things are expensive, but I found it was comparable to Denmark

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There are so many clubs!!! It's awesome

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: All sorts - if you have an interest in anything, I would say pretty confidently that there is a club for it. You can watch hockey games, join painting or knitting clubs, there is language exchange stuff happening, all sorts!

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I took part in a Japanese language table as part of my Japanese course, where you talked to native Japanese speakers once a week, that was really fun. Otherwise, I was part of the photo society, which was also great - but again, it depends on what you're interested in!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Explore Vancouver! There are tons of parks around (Stanley Park, pretty famous, or Van Dusen, Queen Elizabeth, or even Nitobe which is right on campus and free with your UBC card), cool cafés, and beaches (e.g., Wreck Beach, Jericho Beach, Acadia Beach...)
You can go skiing on Grouse Mountain or in Whistler. I also know lots of people went to Banff, Seattle - all over!
It's easy to stay on campus cause it's so beautiful, but try to explore the city as much as you can, too!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy, I just missed good bread. Otherwise it was no problem at all haha!

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Just go up and say hi! It's scary, but you've got nothing to lose in the end. Also joining clubs is a great way to meet local students! Just be a kind human and be curious about the people you are meeting!

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Tipping culture! It's quite high and expected in many places, which I found a bit stressful sometimes

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: People are so kind! Lots of people yell thank you at the bus driver as they are getting off, which I get a kick out off every time it happens. Also lots more small talk, like at the cash - really nice!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) In case you don't get into on campus housing, don't stress - but start looking early for housing off campus! Winter Term 2 goes from Jan to end of April, so housing options for September start going up as early as then. Just be aware of the different timelines, starting to look in July is going to be  quite difficult!
2) Try to balance school and fun! I was quite focused on my classes because I was really enjoying them, but I do wish I had explored a little bit more!
3) Push yourself to get out of your comfort zone, and try all the things you are curious about! It is really easy to say "I'll do it some other time", but the exchange goes by super quickly (classes are only like three months in the end, exams take up most of the last month) so do all you want to do!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
The workload is different compared to Copenhagen, because there are lots of assignments during the semester, instead of only one big exam at the end. It took me a while to adjust to staying on top of everything, but it worked out fine - but just so you are aware of that, you might have to manage your time a bit differently! Also attendance counts towards your grade in some classes, so look carefully at the syllabus!
And explore campus, it's awesome and huge and has so much to offer:)

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting so many nice people from all over, and having so much fun together. For me, the classes I took were in things I was really interested in, and it made me think about where I want to go in the future, both academically and personally, and whether I might switch directions. I felt like I got to overcome a lot of anxieties, and explore the things I loved, which made me a lot happier and open as a person. And taught me that going out of your comfort zone does bring good things!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I think keeping up with all the course work during the semester was a learning curve for me. And finding friends was hard in the beginning, just due to the lack of events offered to meet people. Staying positive things would work out was a challenge, but it did all work out in the end!

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer:
UBC is really big on supporting students, so if you are ever overwhelmed, don't hesitate to talk to the profs, they usually will give you an extension if you need one!
Otherwise, going on exchange was an awesome time, and I think a great opportunity to grow as a person if you let yourself do so. 
There is an ice cream shop called Rain or Shine on campus - my favourite flavour was London Fog, but try anything there, it's delightful!
I hope you have a great exchange if you decide to go with UBC: It is one of my favourites of the things I have done so far:)

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
